title: The sideways blast
teaches: Why Mount St Helens exploded sideways on 18 May 1980: a bulging flank, a landslide, and magma suddenly unloaded

blocks.text: In March 1980, Mount St Helens in southern Washington woke after 123 years of quiet. Small earthquakes began in mid-March, and on 27 March steam explosions blew a crater in the summit ice. Scientists from the US Geological Survey and the University of Washington set up instruments around the mountain. Within a few weeks they saw something alarming: the north side of the volcano was swelling outward.

By late April the bulge on the north flank was 2 kilometres across and had pushed out by more than 100 metres, and it was still growing at about 1.5 to 2 metres a day. Magma was rising into the volcano, but instead of coming up the central vent it was forcing its way into the north flank, wedging it outward like a balloon inflating under a carpet. The flank was getting steeper and less stable. The geologists warned that it might slide, and the areas closest to the mountain were closed.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Mount St Helens reawakened in March 1980 with earthquakes and steam explosions.
Rising magma forced its way into the north flank, which bulged outward 1.5 to 2 m a day.

blocks.text: At 8:32 on Sunday morning, 18 May, a magnitude 5.1 earthquake shook the volcano. The whole bulging north flank broke loose and slid away, the largest landslide in recorded history: about 2.5 cubic kilometres of rock, which rushed down into the valley of the North Fork of the Toutle River and filled it as much as 180 metres deep.

The landslide was the lid coming off. The magma inside the bulge had been holding its water dissolved under the pressure of the rock above, as in lesson 18's conduit, only far shallower. Within seconds that pressure dropped to almost nothing. The gas came out all at once. Bubbles grew until the magma was mostly gas, a froth whose thin walls tore apart into shreds and ash (geologists say it **fragmented**), and the expanding gas flung the pieces outward. Water in the rock around it, hotter than its boiling point but kept liquid by the same pressure (**superheated**), flashed to steam at the same moment. Together they exploded through the gap where the flank had been. Because the opening faced north, the explosion went north too: a **lateral blast**, a ground-hugging cloud of hot gas, rock and ash, faster than the landslide, that overtook it within seconds.

blocks.caption: Mount St Helens from south to north. Rising magma bulges the north flank; when the flank slides away, the pressure on the magma falls and its gas share jumps past the point where it fragments. The bulge is greatly exaggerated.

blocks.text: The blast flattened about 600 square kilometres of forest in a fan up to 30 kilometres north of the volcano. Close to the mountain the trees were stripped away entirely; further out they were snapped off and laid down in rows, all pointing away from the crater. Fifty-seven people died, among them the USGS volcanologist David Johnston, who was watching the mountain from a ridge 10 kilometres to the north and radioed “Vancouver! Vancouver! This is it!” before the blast reached him.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A magnitude 5.1 earthquake triggered the collapse of the bulging flank: the largest landslide on record.
The landslide removed the weight on the magma, which decompressed and exploded sideways through the gap.
The lateral blast flattened about 600 km² of forest and killed 57 people.

blocks.text: The blast was over in a few minutes, but the eruption was not. With the volcano opened up, the main vent blasted a column of ash 24 kilometres high for nine hours; winds carried the ash east, and it darkened towns across eastern Washington at midday. **Pyroclastic flows**, avalanches of hot ash, rock and gas, poured down the north side. Melting snow and ice turned the landslide debris and new ash into lahars that ran down the Toutle River into the Cowlitz and Columbia, wrecking bridges and filling the shipping channel.

When it was over, the volcano was 400 metres lower, with a horseshoe-shaped crater, about 2 by 3.5 kilometres, open to the north. Until 1980, few geologists had seen a volcano fail sideways. Afterwards, they recognised the same horseshoe craters and hummocky landslide deposits at volcanoes around the world, including Mount Shasta, and realised that flank collapse and lateral blasts are a common way for steep volcanoes to erupt.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: After the blast, a plume 24 km high erupted for nine hours, and lahars ran down the Toutle River.
The volcano lost 400 m of height and was left with a horseshoe crater open to the north.
Flank collapses and lateral blasts turned out to be a common way for steep volcanoes to fail.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the sideways blast
blocks.task: Select the best answer for each question

items.ask: Why did the north flank of Mount St Helens bulge in April and May 1980?
choices: Rising magma was forcing its way into the flank and pushing it outward
Glaciers were sliding off the summit
items.why: Magma intruded into the north side instead of rising up the central vent, wedging the flank outward by metres a day.

items.ask: Why did the eruption begin when the landslide happened?
choices: The slide removed the weight of rock that had been keeping the gas in the magma dissolved
The landslide set the rock on fire
items.why: With the pressure suddenly gone, the dissolved gas came out all at once and the magma exploded.

items.ask: Why was the blast sideways rather than straight up?
choices: The opening left by the landslide faced north
items.why: The magma burst out through the gap where the north flank had been, so the blast went north along the ground.

items.ask: Trees in the blast zone were flattened in rows. What could you learn from the direction they point?
choices: Where the blast came from: they point away from the crater
Which way the wind blew the next day
items.why: The blast knocked trees over in the direction it was travelling, so they radiate out from the volcano.

items.ask: How does St Helens connect to lesson 18's conduit figure?
choices: In both, a sudden drop in pressure lets dissolved water come out of the magma and fragment it
In both, runny basalt erupts quietly
In both, the lava flows sideways
items.why: Unloading by a landslide does in seconds what rising up a conduit does more slowly: it lowers the pressure until the foam breaks apart.

summary: **Magma pushed the north flank out.** It bulged 1.5 to 2 m a day through April and May 1980.
**An earthquake set off a giant landslide.** About 2.5 km³ of the flank slid away at 8:32 a.m. on 18 May.
**The slide unloaded the magma.** Its pressure fell, its gas came out, and it exploded.
**The blast went sideways.** It flattened 600 km² of forest north of the volcano.
**The eruption went on for hours.** A 24 km plume, pyroclastic flows and lahars followed.
**Volcanoes often fail this way.** Horseshoe craters elsewhere record similar collapses.
